title: At the Moment of Death, Ten Recitations Continually Joined, Rebirth Is Attained
author: With deep faith and earnest vows
excerpt: the matchless fervor, perseverance, and resolve that burst forth,

inline.s: Ten recitations, continued without a break, accumulate into a nature;
Abandon evil and practice good; in accord with conditions, dissolve karma.
the matchless fervor, perseverance, and resolve that burst forth,
bringing it about that one never neglects them day or night, making the end of life the appointed term.
Firm perseverance
Zhanran
Skill in an art is perfected by diligence and ruined by play; carve without letting go, and even metal and stone can be engraved.

Question: In The Conditions for Rebirth: Ten Recitations Continually Joined at the Moment of Death, it is explained that by the continual joining of ten recitations at death one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss (see in detail
The Conditions for Rebirth: Ten Recitations Continually Joined
). Then how should one cultivate in order to accomplish the continual joining of ten recitations at death?

Answer: To accomplish the continual joining of ten recitations at death, one must accumulate the continual union of ten recitations into a nature and so be unperturbed in the face of peril; at the same time one must abandon evil and practice good, cultivate merit and dissolve karma, so as to avoid the bewitchment of worldly conditions and the entanglements of creditors, and also to prevent the karmic obstacles of death from appearing. Therefore, the essential method for accomplishing the continual joining of ten recitations at death is:

Among them: “ten recitations continued without a break, accumulated into a nature” is the main practice, and “abandon evil and practice good, in accord with conditions dissolve karma” is the supportive practice. One who practices thus has his karma dissolved and his wisdom clear, his obstacles exhausted and his merit exalted; whatever he does is all smooth and successful.
[Accumulated into a nature] through repeated training, one makes the continual union of ten recitations become second nature.
Now I will explain these four lines of the essential method separately as follows:
Single-mindedness (unbroken single-mindedness) has four levels: ten lines not confused, a hundred lines not confused, a thousand lines not confused, at any time not confused (see in detail
Aware Buddha-Recitation (Abridged)
). Practicing according to
Aware Buddha-Recitation (Abridged)
in order to reach the continual union of ten recitations (ten lines not confused) is quite easy — for one who advances step by step and perseveres without giving up.

What is called the continual union of ten recitations is that, in the course of reciting ten lines of the Buddha’s name, the thought of reciting is joined thought after thought without any admixture of false thought. How can one be without false thought? The wondrous method is: awareness! Awareness is the sharp weapon that stills false thought: when one is aware, there is no false thought; if false thought arises, it shows that at that moment awareness has been lost, and one should immediately lift it up again.
Therefore, the book
Aware Buddha-Recitation (Abridged)

is divided into two major parts, the preliminary practice and the Buddha-recitation. In the preliminary practice, through training in “awareness of the action,” one cultivates a focused, continuous, and enduring power of awareness. After laying a solid foundation, one can then give one’s full strength to Buddha-recitation, so as to reach single-mindedness of the held name (unbroken single-mindedness).
Question: How can one directly accomplish the continual union of ten recitations?
Answer: Master Lianchi gave instruction on a wondrous method:
“Let the mind go along the recitation, each word distinct and clear.”

(Yunqi Dharma Compendium) If you keep on with it, you will accomplish the continual union of ten recitations, and then cause it to accumulate into a nature. If you still cannot get hold of this method, it shows your power of awareness is too weak, and you should first study
Essentials of Breathing Buddha-Recitation

in the section on the “preliminary practice” to cultivate the power of awareness. Once the power of awareness is developed, using Master Lianchi’s method to accomplish the continual union of ten recitations is entirely without difficulty. As for the manner of reciting every ten lines, you may recite two lines at a time, making two lines a group, and count five times silently and you have ten lines. When you are familiar with it you need not count; the moment it leaves your mouth it is clearly ten lines. This method both gathers the mind and is simple, and easily accomplishes “ten recitations continually joined, accumulated into a nature.”

Or you may recite the Buddha’s name thus: imagine the mind as a vase of jade and the Buddha’s name as precious beads; as you recite, each bead falls in. Fitly adjust the speed of the Buddha’s name and the interval between the recitations,
and clearly feel

the “falling in” of each bead. When the practice is mature, the Buddha’s name responds to the mind and is naturally continuous (the Buddha’s name not being interrupted by false thought constitutes continuity; it does not necessarily mean there is no interval between recitations of the name).
If you still cannot get hold of this method, it shows your power of awareness is too weak, and you should first study
Essentials of Breathing Buddha-Recitation
in the section on the “preliminary practice” to cultivate the power of awareness. Once the power of awareness is developed, then recite the Buddha’s name this way.
In addition, you may also adopt the method of breathing Buddha-recitation and cause it to accumulate into a nature. (See in detail
Essentials of Breathing Buddha-Recitation
article)
In addition, I will introduce the “gate of single-minded attachment” as follows:
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Pure Land Adornments Praised by the Buddhas says: “Single-minded, not confused.” (See in detail
Commentary on the Sutra Praising the Pure Land Adornments
) Therefore,
when reciting the Buddha’s name, one should attach the mind with the whole heart
, as a child remembers its mother
And one should consciously cultivate the power of attachment; when the power of attachment is strong, the continual union of ten recitations is naturally accomplished.
On this, the Repentance Master Ciyun gave instruction:

Whether going about official business or at home, passing through all kinds of affairs, though hurried, the inner mind never forgets the Buddha, and recollects the Pure Land. Just as worldly people who have an urgent matter fixed in their heart — though they pass through conversation, going and coming, sitting and lying, and all manner of business — are not hindered from secretly recollecting this matter, and it is always vividly present before the eyes.
The mind attached to recollecting the Buddha
should likewise be thus. Or if the attachment is lost, one must draw it back again and again,
so that over time it becomes a nature, and one recollects constantly and spontaneously
. The

Surangama Sutra’s chapter on the bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta’s perfect penetration through Buddha-recitation says: ‘If the minds of sentient beings recollect the Buddha and recite the Buddha, when the present appears and in the future, they will certainly see the Buddha; they are not far from the Buddha, and without relying on expedients they attain the opening of the mind.’ Thus attaching the mind to the Buddha, one naturally and constantly blocks all evil thoughts. If one intends to do evil, because of recollecting the Buddha, the evil cannot be accomplished. Even when one follows evil and does an evil act, the mind is always naturally soft and pliant, as a body that has fragrance is naturally far from stench.

Again, whenever one notices an evil thought rising slightly in the mind, immediately recollect the Buddha; because of the Buddha’s power, the evil thought naturally ceases, just as a person in distress who seeks aid from a forceful and powerful champion will surely be delivered.

Again, when one sees others suffering, with a mind attached to recollecting the Buddha, feel compassion for them and wish them free of suffering. If one is passing sentence, because of the attachment to recollecting the Buddha, a mind of compassion arises; though one follows the kingly law, one should silently make this vow: ‘I carry out the king’s law; this is not my original intention. May you be reborn in the Pure Land, and I vow to rescue you.’

Whatever realm one passes through, whether good or evil, because the mind is attached to the Buddha, it is the true mind that holds sway. Hence the ten great vows of the bodhisattva Samantabhadra say: ‘All evil done does not come to accomplishment; if good karma is done, it all becomes harmonized.’ This is exactly what is meant. Thus continually attaching the mind to the Buddha in the mind, one can accomplish all pure-cause merit.
Original text:
“Whenever going to public
(official business)
or private nurture
(daily life)
, one passes through affairs, and though hurried
(busy)
yet the inner mind never forgets the Buddha, and recollects the Pure Land. Just as worldly people fix their heart on an urgent matter
(an urgent affair)
; though they pass through speech, going and coming, sitting and lying, and all manner of business, yet they are not hindered from secretly recollecting
(not hindered from inwardly recollecting)

, and the former matter is vividly there. The mind that recollects the Buddha should likewise be thus. Or if the thought is lost, one draws it back again and again; over time it becomes a nature, and one recollects constantly and spontaneously. The Surangama Sutra says: ‘If the minds of sentient beings recollect the Buddha and recite the Buddha, in the present and the future, they will certainly see the Buddha; they are not far from the Buddha, and without relying on expedients they attain the opening of the mind.’ Thus attaching the mind, one naturally and constantly blocks
(hinders)

all evil thoughts. If one intends to do evil, because of recollecting the Buddha, the evil cannot be accomplished. Even when following evil and doing an evil act, the mind is always soft and pliant, as a body that has fragrance is naturally far from stench. Again, whenever one notices an evil thought rising slightly in the mind, immediately recollect the Buddha; because of the Buddha’s power, the evil thought naturally ceases — a person in distress who seeks that strong champion will surely be delivered. Again, when one sees others suffering, with a mind recollecting the Buddha, feel compassion for them and wish them free of suffering. If one breaks a case
(passes judgment)
, because of recollecting the Buddha, a mind of compassion arises; though one follows the kingly law, one should secretly
(i.e., silently)

make this vow: ‘I carry out the king’s law; it is not my original intention. May you be reborn in the Pure Land, and I vow to rescue you.’ Whatever realm one passes through, whether good or evil, because the mind recollects the Buddha, all are made in the mind’s thought. Hence the Samantabhadra vow-king says: ‘All evil done does not come to accomplishment; if good karma is done, it all becomes harmonized.’ This is that very meaning. Thus continually recollecting the Buddha in mind, one can accomplish all pure-cause merit.”
(Two Gates of Resolving Doubts and Practicing the Vows for Rebirth in the Pure Land)

This “gate of single-minded attachment” brings the greatest benefit; the point of entry lies in constantly attaching the mind within oneself and never forgetting the Buddha. May one, in all good and evil realms and all manner of affairs, secretly recollect with attachment unbroken — this is what is meant by “The Way is that from which one cannot for a moment
(an instant)
be separated.”
When cultivating the power of attachment, one may raise one line of the Buddha’s name and then be attached for a while. As one practices, gradually lengthen the time of attachment. On the
One-Minute Concentration

webpage there is an audio player: after one minute, a bell sounds. (Right-click the “play button” to set loop-playback mode on the menu or to download.) You can use it to measure how long one line of the Buddha’s name can be held with attachment and without a false thought arising. And use it as a tool to help you practice gradually lengthening the time of attachment. This is the fundamental work of cultivating the power of attachment, extremely important; you must put in hard practice and train it well, making the power of attachment focused, continuous, enduring, and resistant to disturbance, so that a single line of the Buddha’s name is invincible,
and one recollects constantly and spontaneously

. The Chan school’s Fourth Patriarch, Master Daoxin, gave an exceedingly incisive instruction on “guarding oneness without shifting”; this is the essential foundational work for all who study Buddhism, and I hope you will apply it flexibly. (See in detail
Guarding Oneness Without Shifting
article)
[Recollect constantly and spontaneously] following the natural changes of circumstances, the mind is always silently recollecting.

What is called “accumulated into a nature” is that through ceaseless repeated training one makes the continual union of ten recitations become second nature. For this reason, one should recite at every chance and train at every chance, enduring without slacking. Practice as much as possible, and train until the skill is the perfection of refinement, so that at any time and in any place the ten lines of the Buddha’s name flow out in one breath, unmixed with false thought. Remember: one part of effort, one part of harvest; effort never fails the determined heart — you can certainly do it! When sincerity is perfect, even metal and stone open.

In truth, the way of practice is nothing else but one word: “familiarity.” The great general shoots a willow at a hundred paces, and the old oil-seller drips oil through a coin; both are a single “familiarity.” The key points of the “familiarity” formula, stated concretely, are three: first, correct method and sequence; second, a great deal of repeated training (familiarity breeds skill, skill breeds marvel, marvel enters transformation); third, ceaseless pondering, summarizing, and improving. Following this, there is none who does not succeed. (See in detail
Aware Buddha-Recitation (Abridged)
The key to study is: turn what is unfamiliar into familiar; the familiar then naturally turns unfamiliar.

What is called the unfamiliar place is the mind abiding on the Buddha’s name; and the familiar place is the mind’s clinging to the five desires and six dusts, which is the habitual tendency formed since beginningless kalpas and also the root of birth and death’s round. Therefore one who recites the Buddha must focus the mind on one place and not let it scatter,
going along the Buddha’s name, word by word clear, thought after thought continuous
— if a hundred sounds, if a thousand sounds, if ten thousand sounds — single-mindedly reciting, diligent and untiring. Master Yinguang says:
“Whether at home or at a hermitage
(residing in a temple)

, one must respect superiors and be kind to inferiors. Endure what others cannot endure; practice what others cannot practice. Do the work of others; accomplish the good of others. In quiet sitting always reflect on one’s own faults; in idle talk never discuss others’ wrongs. In walking, standing, sitting, lying, dressing and eating, from morning to evening, from evening to morning, one line of the Buddha’s name, never let it be cut off
(do not let it be cut off by false thought)

. Recite in a low voice, or recite silently; apart from reciting the Buddha, do not raise any other thought. If a false thought arises, at that very moment one should cause it to be extinguished. Always bring forth a mind of shame and a mind of repentance. Even if one has cultivation, always feel that my skill is shallow, and do not praise oneself. Only mind one’s own affairs, not others’. Only see good examples, not bad ones. Regard all people as bodhisattvas, and only myself as truly an ordinary man. If you can truly follow what I say and practice, you will certainly be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.”
(Essence of the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang)
[Do not let it be cut off] do not let it be cut off by false thought. Therefore the following passage says:
“If a false thought arises, at that very moment one should cause it to be extinguished.”
Here the “never let it be cut off” is what Master Shandao said:
“Thought after thought continuous.”
(See in detail
Master Shandao’s Teachings on Pure Land
article)
Concerning the importance of “ten recitations continually joined, accumulated into a nature,” Master Daochuo skillfully instructed:

“The wise diligently gather the mind, and at death their thoughts do not scatter. One who does not train in single-minded concentration will certainly scatter at death. When the mind is scattered, it is like a horse that has been trained with a millstone
wèi
millstone)
; if it comes to battle, it wheels about and does not run forward.”

(Translation: the wise, because of diligent gathering of the mind in daily practice, their thoughts at death do not scatter. One who does not practice single-mindedness in daily life will certainly scatter at death. At that time, if the mind is scattered, you cannot make it single-minded even if you want to; this is like a horse trained by turning the millstone — at battle it only goes around and cannot run straight ahead.) (See in detail
Master Daochuo’s Instructions on Pure Practice
article)

The process of “ten recitations continually joined, accumulated into a nature” is precisely the intensive cultivation of the Pure Land karmic cause. The wondrous fruit of intensive Pure Land cultivation, Master Chewu instructed:
While reciting the Buddha, one must let go of the ten thousand conditions and single-mindedly
(the thought of reciting the Buddha)

lift it up. As if saving one’s head from fire, as if mourning one’s parents, as a hen brooding eggs, as a dragon nurturing its pearl; you do not expect a small effect, you do not seek quick success, but only single-mindedly keep reciting like this; this is the supremely profound, wondrous meditation. Thus, in the future, the body and world of the faculties, secretly following the mind,
all transform thought after thought

. This is not something the ordinary mind and fleshly eye can know and see. When the retribution ends and life is done, Amitabha Buddha and all the noble assembly suddenly appear before the eyes, or manifest rare fragrance and heavenly music and all the auspicious signs; only then do people of the world say the Pure Land karmic cause is accomplished. Yet how could the accomplishment of the Pure Land karmic cause be at this very moment?
(The original text is found in detail
Treatise on Buddha-Recitation
in the section on “all transform thought after thought.”
one section)

[The body and world of the faculties] the body formed of the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind). [All the auspicious signs] Master Chewu himself, as early as ten months before his passing, knew in advance the time of his rebirth, and the auspicious signs of his rebirth were many and varied.

In the process of accumulating into a nature, one must make use of every chance! The effect of making use of every chance is especially good; its wonder must be felt much in your own practice — the deeper the insight, the more skillful the use.
Question: How does one “ponder, summarize, and improve”?

Answer: First of all, one must have timely and correct feedback: how did I do in this training session? Which parts were correct, which wrong; which reached the expected goal, which did not; how well did I do in self-discipline and self-restraint? Then aim at the next training plan and the goal to be reached, keeping and developing the good and correcting and improving the bad. In the next training session, implement according to this plan and goal.
[Self-discipline] self-restraint. [Self-restraint] to overcome one’s selfish desires.

Training is hard, even dull — as the saying goes, “The sharpness of a sword comes from the whetting; the fragrance of the plum blossom comes from the bitter cold.” But you can cultivate interest in the practice and the insight. Once interest is cultivated, you will delight in it and enjoy the whole training process. At this point the effort takes hold, the relish abounds, and one cannot stop — straight up the sails to cross the vast sea.

To ensure the continual joining of ten recitations at death, besides accumulating the continual union of ten recitations into a nature, one must also abandon evil and practice good, cultivate merit and dissolve karma, so as to avoid the bewitchment of worldly conditions and the entanglements of creditors, and also to prevent the karmic obstacles of death from appearing. Therefore, abandoning evil and practicing good, and dissolving karma in accord with conditions, are extremely important. Moreover, abandoning evil and practicing good, and dissolving karma in accord with conditions, not only gather merit and avert calamity, but also make the continual union of ten recitations accumulated into a nature easy to accomplish.
Our original teacher Śākyamuni Buddha, speaking with his golden mouth, praised and received by Amitabha Buddha in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, the Amitabha Sutra says:
“One cannot, with little good roots and merit and the conditions of cause, be reborn in that land.
(Translation:
one cannot lack the condition of good roots and merit and be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
See in detail
Commentary on the Amitabha Sutra

[Good roots] namely, the good of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind; because these can give birth to the wondrous fruit, they are called good roots. [The good of the three karmas of body (conduct), speech, and mind] not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct — this is good of body; not lying, not speaking divisively, not using harsh speech, not using idle speech — this is good of speech; not greed, not anger, not delusion — this is good of mind. [Merit] the blessings gained by practicing good conduct. [One cannot, with little good roots and merit and the conditions of cause, be reborn in that land]
the Tang translation (Sutra on the Pure Land Adornments Praised by the Buddhas) says:
“It is not sentient beings of little good roots who shall be reborn in the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitāyus Buddha.”
[Sentient beings] also called living beings, that is, all living things with consciousness.
In the Contemplation Sutra of Immeasurable Life, the Buddha says:
“Those who wish to be reborn in that land
(the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss)

should cultivate the three kinds of merit: first, filially support parents, serve and respect teachers and elders, be compassionate and not kill, and cultivate the ten good deeds; second, receive and uphold the three refuges, fulfill all the precepts, and not violate the rules of conduct; third, bring forth the bodhi mind, deeply believe in cause and effect, read and recite the Great Vehicle, and encourage other practitioners.”
Therefore, one who recites the Buddha must reverently cultivate the three merits of the Pure Land karmic cause, so as to possess the conditions of many good roots and much merit.

[The ten good deeds] ten kinds of good karma: not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not lying, not speaking divisively (not spreading discord), not using harsh speech (not mocking with abusive words), not using idle speech (not speaking meaningless words), not greed, not anger, not delusion (not acting contrary to principle). See in detail
Commentary on the Sutra of the Ten Good Karmic Paths

. [The three refuges] namely the three refuges (the triple refuge): taking refuge in the Buddha, taking refuge in the Dharma, taking refuge in the Sangha. This is taking refuge in the Three Jewels; all Buddhas are the Buddha-jewel, the right Dharma is the Dharma-jewel, the noble sages of the Sangha are the Sangha-jewel. [Bring forth the bodhi mind] bring forth the great mind of seeking the Buddha-way above (to become a Buddha) and of bringing sentient beings below to liberation.
In the Buddha-dharma, the three studies of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, the precepts are the foundation of concentration,
so one who recites the Buddha must strictly uphold the five precepts and the ten good deeds to increase good roots and merit

, and lay the foundation well. If one lacks good roots and merit, one is often bewitched by worldly conditions and entangled by creditors, and “ten recitations continually joined, accumulated into a nature” is hard to accomplish. Therefore, in the Amitabha Sutra the Buddha particularly points out:
“One cannot, with little good roots and merit and the conditions of cause, be reborn in that land.”
In the Sutra of Immeasurable Life the Buddha says:
“Decide for yourself,
upright in body, correct in conduct
doing all the more all good
. Cultivate yourself and purify the body,
wash away the defilement of the mind
. In speech and action be loyal and true, within and without corresponding. One who can save himself, in turn save others, discerning and sincere in seeking,
accumulate the roots of good
. Though hard-working for one lifetime, in a moment, in the next life [one is] born in the Land of Immeasurable Life, with joy without limit.”

[The five precepts] not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not lying, not drinking intoxicants. Not killing is not taking the life of a sentient being; not stealing is not taking others’ property; not committing sexual misconduct is not doing the deeds of lust apart from one’s spouse; not lying is not speaking deceitful words that cheat people; not drinking intoxicants is not taking alcoholic or narcotic substances that stupefy the mind.
Therefore, while diligently reciting the Buddha (the main practice), one must also abandon evil and practice good (the supportive practice), so as to clear away the obstructions on the road ahead.
Master Yinguang says:

“Single-mindedly recite the Buddha, and additionally cultivate worldly good as a supportive practice; practicing according to the method of Yongming and Lianchi, then there is nothing in which one is not benefited. Oneself reforms evil and cultivates good, single-mindedly reciting the Buddha. For all relatives, old friends, and those who have conditions with one, one should also teach them this.”
(Letter Replying to a Layman of Yongjia, Letter Six) And again he says:

“Among the methods of cultivation, only the practice of upholding the Name in recitation is foremost; therefore one should focus especially on faith and vows and the upholding of the Name. And with ‘do no evil, practice all good’ as the supportive practice, then its benefit is great.”
(Letter Replying to the Layman Fang Shengzhao, Letter Six)

[Practicing good] doing some charitable deeds is certainly practicing good, but the most important practicing of good is still to practice the good of one’s own three karmas of body, speech, and mind (
not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not lying, not speaking divisively, not using harsh speech, not using idle speech, not greed, not anger, not delusion

). Therefore, the main point of practicing good is to practice the good of one’s own three karmas of body, speech, and mind. Master Shandao, a manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, gave us a shining example:
“He guarded the precepts, not violating them in the least.”
(See in detail the Records of Pure Land Sages)
In
the online Buddhist Academy of Practice-as-Spoken

's curriculum, the first stage is abandoning evil and practicing good. Through the study of this stage’s courses, one comes to understand the principle, method, and implementation steps of abandoning evil and practicing good, so that the abandonment of evil and the practice of good become more systematic, more thorough, and more solid.

At the same time, one should also cultivate the four immeasurable minds of kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity, and apply them in daily life, to remove suffering and give joy, without resentment or vexation, without anger or hatred.

[The four immeasurable minds] the immeasurable mind of kindness, the immeasurable mind of compassion, the immeasurable mind of joy, the immeasurable mind of equanimity. Giving joy to all sentient beings is called the “immeasurable mind of kindness”; removing the suffering of all sentient beings is called the “immeasurable mind of compassion”; seeing others practice good or be freed from suffering and attain joy, deeply rejoicing, is called the “immeasurable mind of joy”; as for the above three minds, letting them go without clinging, treating enemy and kin equally, not giving rise to love or hate, is called the “immeasurable mind of equanimity.” Therefore these four minds broadly reach immeasurable sentient beings and give rise to immeasurable merit, so they are called the “immeasurable minds.”
Question: I too well know that abandoning evil and practicing good is the foundation of Pure Land study, but I feel it is hard to get a start. What is to be done?
Answer: On the question of how to get a start at abandoning evil and practicing good, I specially recommend a short essay to you:
The Record of Mr. Yu Jingyi Meeting the Kitchen God (Vernacular and Original Text)
(its annotations are found in detail
Commentary on the Record of Mr. Yu Jingyi Meeting the Kitchen God

). I hope you will read it repeatedly, ponder it, experience it, and put it into practice. Among them, the step of implementation is especially important; only through continuous implementation can you grasp the true meaning in the essay; and repeated reading and pondering and experiencing are all for the sake of implementation. If time permits, it would be best to follow
the online Buddhist Academy of Practice-as-Spoken
curriculum, the four courses of the first stage, “abandoning evil and practicing good,” and study them systematically. Likewise, in this course of study, implementation remains the center.
Question: Master Daochuo, in the Collection of Peace and Bliss, instructed:

“If any sentient being, even if he does evil for a whole lifetime, at the end of life with ten recitations continually joined, calls my name, unless he is reborn, I will not attain the right enlightenment.”

Since “even if one does evil for a whole lifetime,” as long as “at the end of life, ten recitations continually joined,” one will certainly be reborn — why then need one abandon evil and practice good?
Answer:
“Even if one does evil for a whole lifetime, as long as at the end of life ten recitations continually join, one will certainly be reborn”

shows that right mindfulness at death (the continual union of ten recitations) is of utmost importance; that is to say, the continual union of ten recitations at death is the sole requirement for rebirth, and as long as ten recitations continually join at death, one can move Amitabha Buddha to come and guide him.

But to reach this requirement, one must in ordinary times accomplish the continual union of ten recitations accumulated into a nature, and abandoning evil and practicing good is a very important supportive condition. Therefore Master Shandao instructed:
“May all people, well pondering within themselves, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying,
must firmly rouse the mind and restrain oneself

, day and night without neglect. When the former thought ends, the next thought is immediately born. Forever enjoying the joy of the unconditioned Dharma, and even till Buddhahood — is that not blissful!”
In the instruction
“firmly rouse the mind and restrain oneself”

means to spur oneself and to restrain oneself. One who indulges himself in evil is unable to “firmly rouse the mind and restrain oneself,” and moreover is not in accord with single-minded recitation of the Buddha, unmixed with false thought.
On this, the Repentance Master Ciyun instructed:
“Thus attaching the mind to the Buddha, one naturally and constantly blocks all evil thoughts. If one intends to do evil, because of recollecting the Buddha, the evil cannot be accomplished.”
Two Gates of Resolving Doubts and Practicing the Vows for Rebirth in the Pure Land

Therefore, one who does not firmly rouse the mind and restrain himself finds it hard to accomplish the continual union of ten recitations accumulated into a nature, and so the continual union of ten recitations at death is not assured. Conversely, if one truly accomplishes the continual union of ten recitations accumulated into a nature, one will not continue doing evil, because
“if one intends to do evil, because of recollecting the Buddha, the evil cannot be accomplished”

Though there are also extremely rare exceptions — one who did evil for a whole lifetime and yet accomplished “at the end of life, ten recitations continually joined.” Such cases are practitioners who in a former life had already achieved a fair measure of skill, and because they had not cut off the delusions of views and thought, turned through the round until this life. In this life they again went astray and did evil the whole of it. At death, under the instruction of a good friend they suddenly came to their senses, repented from the heart, and accomplished the continual union of ten recitations and were reborn. Consider: if it were not for the bodhi mind and the deep skill of a former life, when at death all afflictions press together, how could one suddenly give rise to faith and vows and abruptly accomplish the continual union of ten recitations?

Therefore one must never imitate this, for among ten thousand who are reborn, it is hard to find one such case; and this principle has been taught and discussed by the great masters and patriarchs from ancient times in many, many instructions.
For example,
Master Ouyi
says
“The scripture says that even those who commit the ten evil deeds and the five heinous offenses are able to be reborn [in the Pure Land] —
this is necessarily because in the past they once planted the seed of bodhi

. Without the seed of bodhi, how could they have met with a good spiritual friend? Even if they met a good friend who urged them on, how could they at once give rise to faith and vow and invoke the great Name?”
(Lingfeng Treatise Collection, “A General Discourse at Tianma Temple, Shepu”)
Master Ouyi also says:
The ten recitations at the moment of death
necessarily require deeply planted wholesome roots
. Now, when favorable and adverse circumstances arise, one no longer has right mindfulness
(the thought of Buddha-recitation unmixed with idle thoughts)

— much less at the moment of death. Moreover, when the suffering of death appears, one relies only on the prompting of a good friend; but now, in broad daylight, one still cannot trust and practice the true words of a clear-eyed teacher and good friend!”
(Lingfeng Treatise Collection
“Preface to Practicing the Pure Land Repentance and Releasing Life Society”)

Translation: To accomplish the ten recitations held in succession at death, one must have deeply planted wholesome roots. Now, when favorable and adverse circumstances arise, one no longer has right mindfulness
(the thought of Buddha-recitation unmixed with idle thoughts)

— much less can one maintain right mindfulness at the moment of death. Moreover, in broad daylight, with everything bright and clear, we still cannot trust and practice the true exhortations and teachings of a clear-eyed teacher and good friend; how then could we hope, when the suffering of death arrives, to trust and practice merely with the aid of a good friend’s reminder and guidance?

blocks.text: 4. Dissolving Karma by Going Along with Conditions

inline.s: By
holding the Buddha-name to dissolve karma by going along with conditions,

we train the succession of ten recitations and the cultivation of habit into nature in real combat. Moreover, doing so makes life smoother and more peaceful, and at the same time paves the way for the ten recitations to be held in succession at death, preventing the karma obstructions from appearing at the point of death.

When an idle thought arises, that is the very occasion for turning and dissolving karma; one should immediately seize this opportunity to turn and dissolve karma. Each time one turns it, the karmic seed is weakened a little. Turning it again and again, it is weakened again and again, until at length it is pulled out.

[Karmic seed]The karma created by beings is stored in the ālayavijñāna; because it is able to give rise to manifestation and to blossom and bear fruit, it is called a “seed.” Karmic seeds are also called karmic tendencies, or simply seeds and tendencies; they exert a latent influence — even control — over people’s thoughts and actions.

The patriarchs say: “Go along with conditions to dissolve the old karma; do not add further new calamity.” Therefore, whenever a karmic seed manifests, one should seize this opportunity to weaken it, and even to pull it out. If, on the contrary, one goes along with one’s tendencies, one creates new calamity, and the karmic seed becomes all the stronger; when it erupts later, it is all the harder to control.

When an idle thought arises, this is karma coming to bind the mind; replacing the idle thought with the Buddha-name is the mind turning karma. At all times and in all places, replace idle thoughts with the Buddha-name. If ten lines are not enough, repeat ten more lines; continuing on like this, unceasingly turning karma with the mind, in time the practice deepens and the result is beyond words. The Caigentan says: “At the very point where a thought arises, as soon as you sense it heading toward the road of desire, pull it back onto the road of principle. The instant it arises, be aware; the instant you are aware, turn it back. This is the very pivot of turning misfortune into fortune, of reviving the dead — do not let it pass lightly!”

Remember: along with the stream of manifest thoughts, purify the tendencies of false thinking and of greed, hatred, and delusion. Let not a single thought escape this awareness; let every thought pass through.
When the practice is deep, karma dissolves and wisdom is clear; obstructions end and merit is exalted — the joy of it cannot be expressed in words.
For the way of dissolving karma and removing tendencies, see
the section “The Process of the Mind’s Functions” in Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathāgatagarbha
, and the article
Turning Karma with the Mind
Q: The ten recitations held in succession at death — how do they differ from and how do they relate to the “single-minded, undistracted” [state] spoken of in the Amitabha Sūtra?
A: The ten recitations held in succession at death speak of the moment of death; whereas the single-minded, undistracted [state] spoken of in the Amitabha Sūtra refers to ordinary times (see
the article Single-Minded and Undistracted

). The relationship between the two is this: single-mindedness in ordinary times is the most dependable guarantee of the ten recitations held in succession at death — the saying “train a thousand days for the use of a single hour.” On this point Master Daochuo has a vivid simile: a war horse must be trained in actual combat in ordinary times. If in ordinary times one uses it only to turn a millstone, then in battle it will only go in circles and cannot charge and break the enemy lines. (Master Daochuo’s original words:

“The wise one diligently gathers his mind, so at death his thought does not scatter. One who has not trained the mind to single-pointedness will surely be scattered at death. When the mind is scattered, it is like a horse trained to the mill —
(wèi, a stone mill)
when it comes to battle it wheels about and does not run straight.”
See
Master Daochuo’s Instructions on Pure Practice
Q: What does “of ten thousand who practice, ten thousand reach it” mean?

A: This saying comes from Master Yongming’s Four Selections. In that work the ease and difficulty of investigating Chan and of reciting the Buddha-name are compared. This shows that one who puts an end to birth-and-death through investigating Chan must have a foundation laid in past lives before he can succeed; whereas one who puts an end to birth-and-death through reciting the Buddha-name does not need a foundation laid in past lives. Anyone, as long as his method is correct, as long as he is diligent and persevering, can certainly accomplish the ten recitations held in succession at death and so be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss (putting an end to birth-and-death in this very life). This is what “of ten thousand who practice, ten thousand reach it” means. Please take special note of the word “practice” in “of ten thousand who practice, ten thousand reach it”: one who does not truly practice is not counted among the “ten thousand who reach it.”
Q: Can I accomplish the ten recitations held in succession at death?

A: Your question can be changed into: can I accomplish “the ten recitations held in succession, cultivating the habit until it becomes my nature; abandoning evil and practicing good, dissolving karma by going along with conditions”? For if in your daily life you have already accomplished “the ten recitations held in succession, cultivating the habit until it becomes your nature; abandoning evil and practicing good, dissolving karma by going along with conditions,” then at death you will certainly accomplish the ten recitations held in succession.

To this end, first of all you must make a firm resolution and vow, making rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss the foremost matter of your life. Think of the suffering of illness, think of the suffering of death, and then think of the suffering you would undergo over countless kalpas if you failed to be reborn in this life: what reason is there not to make rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss the foremost matter of your life? The Buddha said:
“Though one toil diligently for a single life, in an instant one is born in the Land of Immeasurable Life, with joy beyond measure.”
(Amitāyus Sūtra)
Then,
with courageous vigor, seize every gap to recite; with courageous vigor, seize every gap to train.

Thus you will certainly accomplish “the ten recitations held in succession, cultivating the habit until it becomes your nature; abandoning evil and practicing good, dissolving karma by going along with conditions.” As the verse says: “The edge of the precious sword comes from the grindstone; the fragrance of the plum blossom comes from the bitter cold.”

You will find that in life there are many things and many reasons that try to drag you away from Buddha-recitation and toward evil (at such a time, not to do evil is to do good, and not to commit the ten evil deeds is to perform the ten wholesome deeds). This is precisely the karma obstruction manifesting, not allowing you to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. This is precisely the test of your faith and vow; this is the very crisis on which rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss depends. Which way to go — evil or good; to recite or not to recite — rests entirely on your faith and vow! As the saying goes: “When two armies meet, the brave one wins.” A person of Buddha-recitation should be a great hero, standing firm between heaven and earth, cutting through thorns and brambles!

[Ten wholesome deeds]The ten wholesome karmas: not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct (three of body); not lying, not slandering, not speaking harshly, not speaking idly (four of speech); not coveting, not being angry, not being deluded (three of mind).

Of course, there are some things that must be done with undivided attention; but how much time in a day is that? Moreover, when a matter requires undivided attention, if you truly give it undivided attention, that is precisely a fine opportunity to train the mind in single-pointedness! It is precisely a reinforcing condition for accomplishing “the ten recitations held in succession, cultivating the habit until it becomes your nature.”

If you practice in accordance with what is said above, you will certainly accomplish the ten recitations held in succession at death and be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. Master Shandao says:
“When the previous thought ends this life, the next thought is born [in the Pure Land]; forever enjoying the bliss of the unconditioned Dharma, even up to Buddhahood — is that not most joyful!”
(On the Special and Mixed Practice of the Pure Karma)

Q: In the essential formula “the ten recitations held in succession, cultivating the habit until it becomes your nature; abandoning evil and practicing good, dissolving karma by going along with conditions,” what is the key point?

A: The ten recitations held in succession are the key point. To recite in unbroken succession at all times and in all places is to be cultivating the habit until it becomes your nature; to abide in the state of unbroken succession is to be abandoning evil and practicing good; when an idle thought arises, to replace it at once with the unbroken ten recitations is to be dissolving karma by going along with conditions. Therefore, the method that demands the least effort and yields the highest result is this: throughout the twenty-four hours, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying, never put down the unbroken recitation. Hence Master Shandao earnestly teaches:
“May all people think carefully: in walking, standing, sitting, and lying, you must rouse the mind and restrain yourself, ceasing neither by day nor by night.”
(On the Special and Mixed Practice of the Pure Karma)
This is the method of great peace and great liberation for the wise. Most essential! Most essential!

[Rouse the mind and restrain yourself]Stir up and discipline yourself. These four words are a mighty weapon for overcoming difficulties and clearing away obstructions. “Restrain yourself”: discipline yourself.
[Ceasing neither by day nor by night]Neither by day nor by night should you stop the succession of thought after thought.

However, note this: if you cannot “never put down the unbroken recitation throughout the twenty-four hours, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying,” then you must find out the reason. In fact, “never putting down the unbroken recitation throughout the twenty-four hours, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying” is not harder than going to work, while rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss surpasses becoming a multimillionaire by no one knows how many times over! But why is it that many who recite the Buddha-name cannot “never put down the unbroken recitation,” yet for a trifle of petty profit they can put up with all manner of grievance and work day and night? The reason is that they are blocked by karma (analyze yourself and observe others, and you will understand how karma obstructs and hinders). This is why those who recite the Buddha-name lay such stress on abandoning evil and practicing good and on observing the precepts as the foundation, for this is the basis of “the ten recitations held in succession, cultivating the habit until it becomes your nature.” Without this foundation, how can one escape the envelopment and entanglement of karma obstruction, how can one achieve concentration of the mind on a single point? This would reduce “the ten recitations held in succession, cultivating the habit until it becomes your nature” to empty talk. On how to abandon evil and practice good and observe the precepts as the foundation, see
the curriculum of the “Online Buddhist Academy of Practice and Teaching”
Q: How, concretely, should one cultivate “the ten recitations held in succession, cultivating the habit until it becomes your nature”?

A: It can be carried out in two ways. On the one hand, continually recite ten lines at a time, making them more and more familiar until utterly familiar. On the other hand, cultivate the power of recollecting the Buddha, making it concentrated, continuous, and enduring. The method is: raise a single line of the Buddha-name, and with concentration, closely and unbrokenly, recollect Amitabha Buddha as a child longs for its mother (
the Buddha-light illumines body and mind, and one gains great empowerment

); when an idle thought is about to arise, raise another line of the Buddha-name, and again with concentration, closely and unbrokenly, recollect Amitabha Buddha as a child longs for its mother; continue on like this. Between the two lines, let no idle thought mix in; the longer the interval between them the better. When in time the practice is deep, then not only are the ten recitations held in succession, but one can sustain a hundred, a thousand, and at any moment keep the succession.
[Power of recollection]The power of single-minded recollection, able to resist interference and temptation. The Sutra of the Buddha’s Bequeathed Teaching says:
“If the power of recollection is firm, though one enter among the thieves of the five desires, one is not harmed by them.”
The Sutra of the Contemplation of the Practice of the Dharma of Universal Goodness says:
“Because the power of recollection is strong, one sees my body.”
[The Buddha-light illumines body and mind, and one gains great empowerment]The Amitāyus Sūtra says:

“Sentient beings who encounter this light have the three stains extinguished, body and mind become gentle, they rejoice and leap, and wholesome thoughts arise. Even those in the most painful places of the three evil destinies, upon seeing this light, all gain rest and no longer suffer. After the end of life, they all attain liberation.”
Master Yinguang’s Eulogy of Mahasthamaprapta says:
“As a child recollects its mother, so recollect the World-Honored One
(Amitabha Buddha)
— straightaway one receives the grace. The mind of cause and the enlightenment of fruit correspond, and at once one returns to the source, gathering the six senses — the wonder is beyond words.”

[Three stains]Another name for the three poisons, namely greed, anger, and delusion. [Three evil destinies]The fire, the knife, and the blood — that is, the three evil realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, the places produced by the various evil karmas of body, speech, and mind. (1) The fire: the hell realm, where beings are constantly tormented by boiling cauldrons and burning furnaces, hence called the fire. (2) The knife: the hungry-ghost realm, where beings constantly suffer the driving pressure of knives and staves, hence called the knife. (3) The blood: the animal realm, where the strong prevail over the weak and devour one another, drinking blood and eating flesh, hence called the blood.
Q: I know I should diligently recite the Buddha-name and I often make resolutions, but it always turns out the opposite; every day passes and I can’t say how. What shall I do?

A: The problem is this: everyone knows he will die, yet in the depths of his mind he always clings to the delusion that he will not die. Hence he is indifferent to death’s daily approach; even if he happens to think of it, he quickly casts the thought aside. Therefore everything he does starts from the assumption that he will not die, and he creates all manner of karma — “all day long he only regrets he has not amassed more, and when at last he has much, his eyes close” is just this case. Still less does he seek the noble path of escaping from death in this life; and even if he is already studying that noble path, he is lazy and self-indulgent. So one should often turn the mind back to reflect upon oneself: have I fallen again into the deluded inversion of clinging to not dying? The ancients often said:
“In reciting the Buddha-name, be diligent and vigorous, as though saving your head from a fire.”
That is to say, the fire on your head is blazing, death is approaching swiftly; Buddha-recitation is to be done hurriedly, eagerly putting out this fire of death —
accomplish the succession of thought after thought before unconsciousness and death overtake you
. Universal Worthy Bodhisattva’s Verse of Warning says:
“This day has already passed, and life diminishes with it, like a fish in shrinking water — this
(this)
— what joy is there? All of you: be diligent and vigorous, as though saving your head from a fire! Always bear in mind impermanence
(always bear in mind the coming of death)
— do not be heedless.”

[Fish in shrinking water]A fish in a pond whose water is daily drying up. [Impermanence]Nothing abides forever; it also refers to death, the demon that seizes the soul. [Do not be heedless]By no means let yourself go in pleasure and indulgence, wasting your spirit and your time.
Therefore, to put an end to birth-and-death, one must make a resolute decision. Master Lianchi has set a shining example for us. (See
Master Lianchi’s “The Brushstroke”
In the early stage of resolving to reform, people all pass through a bottleneck where they hesitate and cannot advance. Let us look at how the sages of old walked out of this predicament. In
Mr. Yu Jingyi’s Encounter with the Kitchen God
there is this passage (in translation):

When Mr. Yu came to know wherein his problem lay, on New Year’s Day of the following year he bowed in prayer to heaven and earth and vowed to reform his past faults thoroughly, abandoning evil and practicing good. He took for himself the sobriquet “the Pure-Minded Man” to show that he would firmly remember his vow: to uproot the evil of the mind.

In those first days of abandoning evil and practicing good, scattered thoughts arose in crowds, slipping in through every gap — now hesitating and unable to advance, now lazy and slack, unable to rouse himself. Time flew by, yet he remained the same as before. Therefore, before the image of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva set up in his family shrine, Mr. Yu kowtowed until the blood flowed, and made this earnest vow: “May my good thoughts be forever pure and my power of good be diligent; if I relax in the least in abandoning evil and practicing good, may I fall forever into hell.” Every morning at dawn he reverently recited “Great Compassionate, Great Merciful Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva” a hundred times, to beg the Bodhisattva’s protection.
From then on, in every word and deed, in every thought and moment, it was as though gods and demons stood at his side, and he dared not deceive his own mind or give way to license.

Whatever could help others and benefit the public, great or small, whether he was busy or at leisure, whether people knew of it or not, whether his own strength sufficed or not, he did it joyfully, bending every effort to bring it to completion. Following the circumstances, adapting to the person, the time, and the place, he used various means to plant merit in secret. And with the principles of ethics, virtue, diligence, humility, forbearance, and the law of cause and effect, he exhorted and instructed everyone he met. Working thus all day long, he still felt he had not done enough. On the last day of each month he tallied up his words and deeds of that month, then wrote them into a memorial and reported them before the tablet of the Kitchen God.
When his practice became thoroughly familiar
, every movement was accompanied by ten thousand good deeds, and in stillness not a single thought arose.

A person of Buddha-recitation should likewise make a resolute decision and keep his vow, so that in every word and deed, in every thought and moment, it is as though gods and demons stood at his side, and he dares not deceive his own mind or give way to license. Time flies, and life is fleeting — do not take it lightly, amusing yourself and wasting your hours, only to repent endlessly!

Just think: to accomplish something in this world — how arduous, how difficult! And the affair is not in your own hands; you must beg help from others and prevail over competitors. But rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss neither requires begging from others nor involves competition —
you need only do your own due effort!
So Master Yinguang instructs:
“Only return home, and when you return it is gained; who contends for the wind and moon of the homeland?”
Master Shandao instructs:
May all people think carefully: in walking, standing, sitting, and lying, you must rouse the mind and restrain yourself, ceasing neither by day nor by night
(neither by day nor by night should you stop the succession of ten recitations)
— when the previous thought ends this life, the next thought is born. Forever enjoying the bliss of the unconditioned Dharma, even up to Buddhahood — is that not most joyful!”
(On the Special and Mixed Practice of the Pure Karma)

[Rouse the mind and restrain yourself]Stir up and discipline yourself. These four words are a mighty weapon for overcoming difficulties and clearing away obstructions. Here “rouse” is the same as “excite,” to stir up and spur on. “Restrain yourself”: discipline yourself.
Our original teacher Śākyamuni Buddha earnestly exhorts us in the Amitāyus Sūtra:
“Each of you should diligently strive and diligently seek it for yourself; you will surely transcend and go on to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Why not cast aside the affairs of the world and diligently practice, seeking the Way and virtue? There you may gain the supremely long life, with happiness and joy without end.”
“Though one toil diligently for a single life, in an instant one is born in the Land of Immeasurable Life, with joy beyond measure.”
[Way and virtue]The true Dharma is called the Way; having attained the Way and not losing it is called virtue.

Q: My succession of ten recitations was going just fine, but somehow I have badly regressed! No matter how I recite, it won’t do; distress, exhaustion, and drowsiness come one after another, and even false imaginings circle about and won’t go away. What should I do?

A: This is not a great regression; rather, the practice has reached the most critical juncture: the effort has taken hold and has pressed upon and roused the karmic seeds stored in the ālayavijñāna over countless kalpas, so that they leap out. You must calmly and steadily meet the battle. The way to deal with them is one word: endure. Use the ardor and perseverance kindled by true faith and earnest vow to endure through it; to endure past it is victory! So at this time you must rouse your spirit and never let go of the Buddha-name. “You fight your fight; I fight mine” — as long as I attend to my own Buddha-name, my boat will not capsize! “However weary in body and mind, the vow to seek the Pure Land never retreats.” Although to endure one must grit one’s teeth, this chiefly means the unshakable confidence and the determination never to bow to difficulty. But in the concrete doing, it does not hurt to add a touch of light humor, and even to smile, to see what it can do to me! Remember, this is the darkness before dawn. Endure past this barrier, and it is a great victory.
[The karmic seeds of countless kalpas pressed upon and roused]Mr. Jiang Weinong has this passage of personal experience in his Reply to Mr. Mao Jingquan:
I recall that five years ago, your servant
(Mr. Jiang Weinong speaking of himself)
was in Beijing. One day, just as I was reciting the Buddha-name
(one day, just when I was reciting the Buddha-name)
, suddenly a great evil thought arose. I was terrified, and my sweat poured out like a wash
(streaming with sweat)
— I even dared not do my practice for several days. Afterwards I thought
(afterwards, thinking to myself)
, never in my life have I had such a thought; whence did this thought come? It is likely
(it is probably the karmic seeds stored in the ālayavijñāna over many lives)
I was a little comforted
(somewhat comforting myself)
. But in the end I still doubted and could not settle it
(yet I could not determine what the matter really was)
. Later I went to bow to Venerable Di
Lao
(later I asked the Venerable Dixian)
, and Venerable Di said: ‘This is the seeds of many lives
(these are the karmic seeds of many lives)
, now pressed out by the power of the Buddha’s transformation;
by working on from here, you can pull them out root and all
(you can root out these karmic seeds)
Master Hanshan, in
Reply to Zheng Kunyan of the Central Censorate, has this instruction as well:

If the effort reaches the point where it has taken hold, and the external distractions do not enter, then only the internal afflictions of the mind suddenly arise on all sides without cause. Or desire bursts out, or the mind becomes vexed, or all manner of obstructions arise, till the mind is weary and the strength exhausted and there is nothing to be done about it. These are the tendencies and seeds (also called karmic seeds) stored in the ālayavijñāna over countless kalpas, today pressed and roused by the effort, all manifesting. This is the most critical juncture: you must be clear in your own mind, first recognize them and see through them, and by no means be enveloped by them, by no means be manipulated by them, by no means take them as real. You need only rouse your spirit, exerting courage and vigor, and take up the original huatou you are investigating. If the thoughts of desire and affliction still circle about and will not leave, then pursue them relentlessly at the very place where they arise: “Here originally there is no such matter; ask whence it comes? What, in the end, is it?” You must surely see its end. Pressing it thus, you will cause even spirits and demons to weep, and their traces to vanish and hide. You must chase them down utterly, killing them off, leaving not a single thread.
Striving thus, you will naturally see good news.
(The original text is found in
Essentials of Chan and Pure Land
, in the section “Essentials of Cultivation and Realization.”)

Furthermore, when distressed (or weary, or drowsy), carefully observe just what kind of a feeling it is. When you observe it thus, the distress (or weariness, or drowsiness) gradually becomes less intense and less disturbing, and the mind slowly becomes tranquil.
However tired the body, however weary the mind — the vow to seek the Pure Land shall never decline.
Q: What is the mind of renunciation?

A: The mind of renunciation is the mind that turns away from the Sahā world and escapes the cycle of birth and death. It is the prime mover of all practice. The Pure Land school often says, "Joyfully seek the Land of Ultimate Bliss; renounce the Sahā world." To renounce the Sahā world is precisely the mind of renunciation. Slackness in practice, fear of hardship, and clinging to worldly affairs and sensual pleasures — all these are concrete signs that the mind of renunciation is weak. Therefore, cultivating the mind of renunciation is a most important link in the study and practice of the Pure Land school. On this point the patriarchs and great masters through the ages have left many important teachings; for details, see the article
"Joyfully Seeking the Pure Land, Renouncing the Sahā World"

The key to cultivating the mind of renunciation is this: see through, and let go. Note, however, that letting go does not mean giving up or running away. Toward the realities of life, one who recites the Buddha-name should have the courage to face them and the courage to shoulder them. Doing his duty and giving his best in what he ought to do, he yet "does not grasp at marks, and remains thus unmoved." This too is practice — and a most extraordinary practice. Pressing on through the tempering, his grade of rebirth will surely be high. (See
The Buddhadharma in the World

Q: Master Ouyi's Essential Explanation of the Amitabha Sutra says: "Q: Ten thoughts or a single thought alike attain rebirth, so why must there be seven days? A: If there were not the work of seven days in ordinary times, how could there be ten thoughts or a single thought at the end of life?" What does this mean?

A: The "seven days" here refers to single-mindedness, undistracted. What this passage means is: "The student asked again: 'The ten thoughts at the end of life, or a single thought held in succession, can each bring rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; why then must there be the work of reciting the Buddha-name to the point of single-mindedness, undistracted?' The answer: 'If there were not the work of single-mindedness, undistracted, in ordinary times, how could there be the ten thoughts, or the single thought held in succession, at the end of life?'" In ancient writing, the use of allusion (the citing of classical allusions) was favored; the allusion of "seven days" comes from the Buddha Speaks of the Amitabha Sutra:

"If there be good men or good women who hear of Amitabha Buddha and hold fast to his name, whether for one day, for two days, for three days, for four days, for five days, for six days, or for seven days, single-minded and undistracted, then when such a person is about to die, Amitabha Buddha and all the holy host will appear before him; when that person ends his life, his mind will not be inverted, and he will attain rebirth in Amitabha Buddha's Land of Ultimate Bliss."
For the annotations on how one attains single-mindedness, undistracted, from one day up to seven days, see
Commentary on the Amitabha Sutra
